title: Lawrence Brown, Mingus and a band of individual stars
summary: Greer praises Lawrence Brown, says Mingus was temperamental, and calls the band a group of individual stars.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: exaggeration, Lawrence Brown was the greatest trombone player I ever heard in my life. Lawrence Brown, you remember Lawrence Brown trying to make -- well, they were always looking for a ofay--- king --/today in prizefighting, but anyway Lawrence Brown, I know one time on a recording session, if Barney Bigard, on clarinet, if he didn't show or was late for the recording, he would give Lawrence Brown a clarinet part. Ever heard of that, a trombone player playing a clarinet part?

And he would run it clean as a whistle. We were in California making a picture and Tommy Dorsey, he said to me, I'll never forget said 'That's the greatest trombone player in the world.' And Lawrence Brown didn't know what he could do, you better believe it. Barney, and a bass player -- Charlie Mingus just died.
He played with us. He was a hard character to get along with.

I don't know. Temperament. I got along beautifully with him, but he wasn't good for a bunch of guy's organization because he would create a lot of little disturbances. He wasn't -- and the thing about Duke's band we had a band of individual stars. They could stand on their own. On their own two feet, but as a team, they were just like this.
